case_study_insert.main_stem: Thistle & Loom Retail (TLR) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2016 by Fiona Thistlewaite, the business sells knitwear and lifestyle clothing through its own e-commerce website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TLR plans to invest $420,000 in a new automated e-commerce fulfilment centre with computer stock control, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 24,000 units a year. TLR faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 16% and its online return rate is 14%, with picking errors rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and E-commerce Report — Q3 2025: The online store fulfilled 6,200 orders last quarter with a picking error rate of 2.1%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Product returns ran at 14% of orders, costing an average $22 per parcel. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average delivery time is 4.1 days. A survey of 500 online fashion shoppers found that 71% value fast delivery and 58% would switch brand after a returns problem. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 60 staff have not been trained on the new computer stock-control system; off-the-job courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thistle & Loom Retail as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.0% from $13.00 to $13.65 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Wholesale cotton and synthetic fabric input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while online fashion consumer spending grew 4.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: TLR plans to finance part of its $420,000 expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TLR of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $120,000 of retained profit costs TLR no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the firm already carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $300,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid to the lender can absorb the 9.5% rise in cotton and fabric input costs, letting TLR hold its $30.00 selling price and protect the $12.00 contribution per unit on each of its 24,000 units. This matters when the online return rate is already 14% and each returned parcel costs an average $22.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the security and repayment risk of the bank loan, so the automated fulfilment centre is not exposed to repossession if demand for the new range disappoints. It also preserves Fiona Thistlewaite's ownership and control: no lender can impose covenants on how the e-commerce operation is run, which fits the flat, democratic structure and lets TLR react quickly to the 16% labour turnover problem without seeking external approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TLR's retained profit, bank loan, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: TLR is launching a new knitwear range through its e-commerce website. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should TLR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A national TV advert would build mass awareness of the new knitwear range quickly across the whole country, which could drive traffic to the e-commerce website. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 60-person retailer funding a $420,000 fulfilment centre, and most viewers are outside TLR's target online fashion segment, so spend wastage would be severe. TV also gives poor tracking of clicks and sales.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper, reaches a defined regional audience and suits time-limited launch messages. Its weakness is narrow geographic reach: TLR sells through a national e-commerce website, so local listeners cannot deliver the order volumes needed to utilise 24,000 units of capacity, and there is no direct route from hearing an ad to buying online.

Social-media influencer marketing: Fashion and lifestyle influencers reach precisely the online fashion shoppers TLR surveyed, where 71% value fast delivery and 58% would switch brand after a returns problem. Influencer posts link straight to the website, are measurable, cost far less than television, scale nationally unlike radio, and can demonstrate the new range visually. Credibility risk exists if an influencer is poorly matched, and results build more slowly than a TV burst.

Recommendation: TLR should choose social-media influencer marketing. It targets the exact online segment at low cost, is measurable, and can showcase knitwear visually while reinforcing the reliable-delivery message the survey demands. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with $180,000 fixed costs and a $300,000 loan; local radio is rejected because its regional reach cannot serve a national website. TLR should pair influencers with modest on-site promotions rather than either rejected mass medium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to TLR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to TLR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to TLR with a justified recommendation that explains why television and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: TLR's labour turnover has reached 16% and its online return rate is 14%. Explain two benefits for TLR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its fulfilment team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 employees a real voice in how the new fulfilment centre is organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help design picking routines are more likely to stay, directly tackling the 16% labour turnover and reducing the disruption that contributes to the 2.1% picking error rate.

Point 2: Consulting the people who handle returns daily generates practical ideas for cutting the 14% return rate, for example clearer size guidance or better packing, which lowers the average $22 cost per returned parcel. Higher involvement also builds commitment and reduces absence, protecting output of 24,000 units while the $420,000 automated centre beds in, and it fits TLR's flat structure because decisions do not have to pass through many layers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TLR's turnover, return rate and output.

questions.question_text: TLR must train 18 of its 60 staff on the new computer stock-control system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TLR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the fulfilment line is directly relevant to TLR's own computer stock-control system and packing standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn. That protects the 2.1% picking error rate and the effort needed to cut the 14% return rate during the $420,000 centre rollout. The drawbacks are that trainers are themselves operators whose work slows, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no external certificate if customers ever ask for formal records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 18 staff, costing $13,500 in total (18 × $750) — small against the $420,000 investment. It removes staff from the line, however, reducing short-term capacity when labour turnover is already 16%, and the generic content may not match TLR's exact stock-control settings, so follow-up coaching would still be required.

Decision: TLR should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups later for the most senior operators. It is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while the return rate is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $13,500 and withdrawing 18 of 60 staff would disrupt the design and packing schedule, and TLR can add college visits once the new centre stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TLR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to TLR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods applied to TLR with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the stock-control system.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TLR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($30.00 − $18.00) = $180,000 ÷ $12.00 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $30.00 − $18.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TLR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 15,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 24,000 units to confirm the online operation is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 9,000 units before the $420,000 fulfilment centre would cease to cover costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets managers model a discount: a $2 price cut to $28.00 would leave $10.00 contribution, so they can judge whether extra orders would still cover the $180,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the volume needed to service the $300,000 bank loan, checking that 24,000 units generates enough contribution before further capital is committed.
4. Unit cost data ($180,000 ÷ 24,000 units + $18.00 = $25.50 a unit) lets managers benchmark each quarter and investigate the 14% return rate and $22 per-parcel cost as drivers of avoidable cost.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 9,000 units versus 24,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $180,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $300,000 bank loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $25.50 to tackle the 14% return rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TLR's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TLR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $75,000 + $80,000 + $45,000 = $200,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50; for 2025 it is $200,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.00. The stricter 2024 measure is ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75; for 2025 it is ($200,000 − $75,000) ÷ $100,000 = $125,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.25.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has clearly strengthened. The broader measure rose from 1.50 to 2.00 as current liabilities fell from $120,000 to $100,000 while current assets rose from $180,000 to $200,000. The stricter measure, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.75 to 1.25, so TLR no longer depends on selling stock to meet short-term debts — important while it services a $300,000 bank loan and funds a $420,000 fulfilment centre. The stronger of the two signals is the stricter measure, because it still exceeds 1.0 without relying on inventory that may be slow to sell given the 14% return rate. The main residual risk is trade receivables rising from $60,000 to $80,000, tying up cash; if online shoppers or wholesale customers pay late, the improvement could unravel, and inventories fell from $90,000 to $75,000, which may limit stock available for peak fashion demand.

Conclusion: TLR's liquidity has improved. Both the broader measure (1.50 to 2.00) and the stricter measure (0.75 to 1.25) show stronger short-term solvency, and the gain does not rest on inventory. The outstanding concern is rising trade receivables, so TLR should tighten credit control while proceeding with the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TLR of introducing an automated computer stock-control system in its new fulfilment centre.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Computer stock control gives real-time inventory counts, which directly attacks the 2.1% picking error rate and the 14% return rate by ensuring the correct item and size is dispatched. Faster, more accurate fulfilment supports the 71% of surveyed shoppers who value fast delivery and the 58% who would switch brand after a returns problem, protecting the $30.00 selling price and the 24,000-unit output that underpins the $420,000 centre.

Disadvantage: The software and scanners add to the $180,000 fixed costs and must be integrated with the e-commerce website, requiring staff training — the insert shows 18 of 60 staff still need training and college courses cost $750 each. If the system fails or data is entered wrongly, online orders could be delayed, worsening the 4.1-day delivery time and increasing returns at the very moment TLR is trying to reduce them.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TLR's error rate, returns, survey data and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 5.0% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in fabric input costs will affect TLR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.25%): If TLR's $300,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.5% of $300,000 = $1,500 a year (0.005 × $300,000). That is modest next to $180,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero. Higher base rates may still make consumers more cautious about discretionary fashion spending and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $420,000 centre, but TLR can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.0%, to $13.65 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in packing and fulfilment, this feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 24,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 400 units per worker. A wage rise is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Fabric input-cost inflation (9.5%): The insert never decomposes the $18.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $18.00 = $1.71 a unit; at 24,000 units a year this is about $41,040 a year (24,000 × $1.71). Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution per unit materially, and the 14% return rate means some of this cost is wasted. TLR can recover part through price negotiations and better stock control, but the pressure is continuous.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,000 units and directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $420,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is around $1,500 a year on a fixed-sum loan and can be hedged, and the wage effect depends on 400-unit productivity that management can influence through training.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TLR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TLR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to TLR with a well-justified judgement that fabric input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
